script.opening: “Morning, doctor. It’s a bit awkward, this. Since the heart attack, things haven’t been… working, in the bedroom. My wife said I should ring. But I don’t want another tablet on my list — I’m rattling already.”

facts.text: “Getting it up, and keeping it. It started a bit after the heart attack but the last four months it’s been bad.” If asked about the bisoprolol change: “The heart doctor upped one of them around then — the beta one, I think.”
“Still sometimes in the morning, but weaker.” Interest in sex is the same as ever.
No chest pain, no breathlessness, no palpitations. Walks 30 minutes a day, climbs the stairs at work fine. “Did all the rehab classes.”

facts.topic: Fears (if asked how he and his wife feel about it)
facts.text: “To be honest, we’re both a bit scared. What if I have another one… you know, during?”

No urinary symptoms, no penile pain or curvature, no testicular lumps. Married 30 years, wife Manjit, no other partners. Mood good. Drinks a couple of beers at the weekend. Stopped smoking at the heart attack.

facts.topic: Online tablets (only if asked about anything bought online, over the counter or from abroad)
facts.text: “Er… yes. I got some blue tablets off a website three weeks ago. Took two. They worked, but I had a pounding headache and went red, and once I felt like I was going to pass out when I stood up.” Seven left in the van. Doesn’t know the dose. If asked about the GTN: “It’s in the van too — I’ve not used it since the rehab.”
“I didn’t want it on my record. And I don’t want more pills — I’m on six already.” Worried about his medical record being seen by insurers (it is not shared without consent).

Be embarrassed and brief at first; open up if the doctor is matter-of-fact. Mention the online tablets only if asked. If the doctor explains the danger with the heart spray calmly, be shocked and agree to stop them. If offered a prescription straight away, say you would rather not add a tablet. If the doctor suggests reviewing the bisoprolol first, be pleased.

worked.txt: “This is really common after a heart attack — the same arteries are involved, and some heart tablets play a part. Thank you for raising it.”
“Have you tried anything yourself — tablets from a chemist, online, or from abroad?”

“Those tablets and your heart spray together can drop your blood pressure dangerously. If you’ve taken one in the last day and get chest pain, don’t use the spray — call 999 and tell them what you’ve taken.”
“You’d rather not add a tablet — so the first step is asking your heart team whether we can bring the bisoprolol back down, which may help on its own.”
“If you can walk briskly or manage two flights of stairs without chest pain — which you can — sex is generally safe for your heart.”

f.learning: Erectile dysfunction after MI is usually multifactorial: vascular disease, medicines (beta-blockers, thiazides), anxiety about exertion, and relationship strain. Always ask about medicines bought online or over the counter — unregulated “herbal” or generic products often contain undeclared or variable doses of PDE-5 inhibitors. PDE-5 inhibitors are absolutely contraindicated with nitrates (GTN, isosorbide) and nicorandil because of profound hypotension; sildenafil SPCs also list recent MI or stroke and hypotension below 90/50 as contraindications. After an uncomplicated MI, sexual activity is usually safe once the patient can manage moderate exertion without symptoms. NICE suggests continuing a beta-blocker for 12 months after MI in people without reduced LVEF and then discussing whether to stop — a natural point to review bisoprolol with cardiology. Respecting a patient’s preference for fewer medicines often means reviewing what he already takes before adding something new.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG185 Acute coronary syndromes (2020) · NICE CKS Erectile dysfunction (accessed 2026) · SPC: sildenafil
knowledge.summary: Find the online tablets and the GTN, explain the interaction, stop them, review the beta-blocker with cardiology, and reassure about sex after MI.

points.t: Gradual onset, preserved morning erections and libido suggest vascular or drug-related causes; sudden onset with situational loss suggests psychogenic. Ask about relationship, mood, anxiety about exertion, genital symptoms, LUTS, smoking, alcohol, drugs and all medicines including online purchases.
Beta-blockers (dose-related; nebivolol may be less implicated), thiazides, spironolactone, SSRIs, antipsychotics, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, opioids. Timing with a dose change is a strong clue.

Contraindicated with nitrates or nicorandil (no GTN within 24 hours of sildenafil or vardenafil, 48 hours of tadalafil). SPC contraindications also include recent MI or stroke, hypotension below 90/50, and severe hepatic impairment. Caution with alpha-blockers. Usual adult dose: sildenafil 50 mg about 1 hour before sexual activity, adjusted to 25–100 mg, maximum once daily (NICE/SPC; check the SPC and local formulary; SPC: sildenafil).
Products from unregistered websites may be counterfeit or contain unknown doses. Advise stopping them and returning them to a pharmacy; report suspected adverse reactions on the Yellow Card scheme.

HbA1c, lipid profile, U&E; morning total testosterone (repeat if low) when ED is associated with reduced libido or if the PDE-5 inhibitor fails; consider PSA only with appropriate counselling. Offer genital examination.

NICE NG185: consider continuing a beta-blocker for 12 months after MI if LVEF is not reduced, then discuss stopping; continue indefinitely if LVEF is reduced. Any earlier change should be agreed with cardiology.

model.text: Good morning, Mr Sandhu, it’s Dr Ahmed. Are you somewhere you can talk privately? What would you like to discuss?
Since the heart attack, things haven’t been working in the bedroom. But I don’t want another tablet.
Thank you for raising it — it’s very common after a heart attack and usually something we can help with. Can I ask a few questions?
When did it start, and is it getting an erection or keeping it? Do you still wake with erections? And how is your interest in sex?
Bit after the heart attack, much worse the last four months. Both. Mornings sometimes. Interest is fine.
Four months ago — was that when the heart doctor increased your bisoprolol? And any chest pain or breathlessness when you exert yourself?
Yes, around then. No pain — I walk half an hour a day.
Have you tried anything yourself — tablets from a chemist, online or from abroad?
Some blue tablets off a website. Took two. Worked, but I got a thumping headache and nearly fainted once.
Thank you for telling me. Do you still have the heart spray, the GTN?

This is important. Those tablets and the spray together can make your blood pressure fall dangerously. Website tablets can also contain unknown doses. Please stop them and take them to a pharmacy. If you’ve had one in the last day and get chest pain, don’t use the spray — call 999 and tell them.

I think a few things are adding up: the arteries, the bisoprolol increase, and probably some worry. As you’d rather not add a tablet, I’ll ask your heart team whether we can bring the bisoprolol back down, and whether a prescribed tablet like sildenafil would be safe for you now. I’ll also check your sugar, cholesterol and kidneys.
model.why: Multifactorial explanation; respects preference; advice and guidance; bloods

model.text: And is it actually safe — sex, I mean? We’re both scared.

If you can walk briskly and climb two flights of stairs without chest pain, sex is generally safe for your heart. Don’t change your heart tablets yourself. I’ll call you when I hear from cardiology — and if you and Manjit would like, there’s counselling that helps couples with this. What will you do with the tablets in the van?

pitfalls.intro: Many candidates prescribe sildenafil or simply reassure. The safety issue sits in what he has already done.

items.fail: Never asks about medicines bought online or over the counter.
items.why: Misses dangerous use of unregulated PDE-5 tablets alongside GTN.
items.fix: Ask routinely in any ED consultation.

items.fail: Tells him to stop the bisoprolol.
items.why: Seven months post-MI; changes should be agreed with cardiology.
items.fix: Seek advice and guidance; keep medicines unchanged meanwhile.

items.fail: Prescribes sildenafil despite his clear preference.
items.why: Ignores his wish to avoid more medicines — the reason he went online.
items.fix: Offer the beta-blocker review first, with a prescribed option if needed.
